title: DOES GOD REALLY EXPECT YOU TO FORGIVE SOMEONE WHO ISN’T EVEN SORRY?
paragraphs: DOES GOD REALLY EXPECT YOU TO FORGIVE SOMEONE WHO ISN’T EVEN SORRY?

They shattered your trust, never admitted what they did, and walked away as though nothing happened. Now you’re being told that Jesus commands you to forgive them. But is that actually what Scripture teaches—or have we confused forgiveness with something God never asked us to do?
There is a particular kind of pain that comes from being hurt by someone who refuses to acknowledge the wound.
Not just the betrayal.
Not just the lies.
Not even the sleepless nights when your mind keeps replaying conversations, wondering whether you missed the warning signs.
It is watching the person who broke something inside you continue living as though nothing happened.
They laugh. They post pictures. They go to church. Sometimes they even quote Bible verses about love, peace, and forgiveness.
Meanwhile, you are still trying to understand how someone could do so much damage and feel so little responsibility.
And then somebody tells you something that makes the wound even deeper.
“You’re a Christian. You have to forgive.”
Perhaps they quote Jesus.
Perhaps they remind you that bitterness is dangerous.
Perhaps they suggest that your unwillingness to pretend everything is fine means you are spiritually immature.
And suddenly, you are carrying two burdens.
The pain of what somebody did to you.
And the guilt of wondering whether God is disappointed because you are still hurting.
But what if the biblical answer is more profound than either extreme?
What if Jesus really does command you to forgive, yet never commands you to call evil good, abandon wisdom, restore trust without evidence, or expose yourself to repeated harm?
And what if one small Greek word helps us understand something Christians have argued about for generations?
Stay with me.
Because the answer is not simply about whether someone deserves your forgiveness.
It is about what the cross of Jesus Christ actually requires of your heart—and what it does not require you to surrender.
The first thing we must understand is that Jesus never treated sin as something insignificant.
He did not come into the world to convince wounded people that their suffering was imaginary.
He came because sin was so serious that nothing less than His own sacrifice could accomplish our redemption.
Think about that.
The cross does not minimize evil.
The cross reveals how terrible evil really is—and how astonishing God's mercy can be.
When Jesus taught His disciples about forgiveness, He said something that deserves careful attention.
In Luke 17:3–4, He declared:

“Take heed to yourselves: If thy brother trespass against thee, rebuke him; and if he repent, forgive him. And if he trespass against thee seven times in a day, and seven times in a day turn again to thee, saying, I repent; thou shalt forgive him.” (KJV)
Read those words carefully.
Jesus did not say that the injured person must deny the offense.
He said, “rebuke him.”
He did not say repentance was irrelevant to the restoration of a broken relationship.
He said, “if he repent, forgive him.”
And He did not place an arbitrary limit on how often a genuinely repentant person could be forgiven.
He commanded repeated forgiveness.
In the Greek text, the phrase “if he repent” is:
ἐὰν μετανοήσῃ — ean metanoēsē

The verb metanoeō means to repent, to change one's mind or disposition. In the biblical context, repentance is not merely experiencing embarrassment over consequences. It involves turning away from wrongdoing toward what is right.
And the word translated “forgive” is:
ἄφες — aphes
It comes from aphiēmi, a verb that can mean to release, send away, remit, or forgive, depending on context.
These words matter.
But we must be careful.
Greek vocabulary does not automatically settle every theological question about forgiveness. Meaning also comes from the surrounding passage and the whole teaching of Scripture.
Luke 17 clearly connects the command to forgive a repentant offender with the offender's repentance.
Yet this is not the only passage Jesus gave us.
And this is where the conversation becomes uncomfortable.
Because the same Jesus who spoke about repentance also commanded His followers to love their enemies.
Not merely tolerate them.
Love them.
In Luke 6:27–28, Jesus said:
“But I say unto you which hear, Love your enemies, do good to them which hate you, Bless them that curse you, and pray for them which despitefully use you.” (KJV)
Notice what Jesus did not say.
He did not say, “Love your enemies once they apologize.”
He did not say, “Pray for those who hurt you after they admit they were wrong.”
He commanded a kind of love that does not wait for the offender to become deserving.
That changes everything.
Because now we must distinguish two realities that Christians sometimes use the same word to describe.
There is the inward posture of releasing vengeance, refusing to nurture hatred, and entrusting justice to God.
And there is the relational act of granting forgiveness in response to repentance, with the possibility of restoring fellowship.
These realities are closely connected, but they are not identical.

Christians disagree about whether the first should technically be called forgiveness or a readiness to forgive. Some understand forgiveness itself as an unconditional release of personal resentment. Others emphasize that the full relational granting of forgiveness is conditioned upon repentance, particularly in Luke 17:3.
Both perspectives must wrestle seriously with the same biblical commands.
We are commanded to love our enemies.
We are forbidden to take personal revenge.
We are commanded to forgive as people who have received mercy.
And we are also commanded to confront sin, practice discernment, and pursue truthful reconciliation.
Scripture does not give us permission to ignore one command in order to obey another.
Perhaps this is where you have been struggling.
You thought forgiveness meant opening the door again.
You thought forgiveness meant answering the phone whenever they called.
You thought forgiveness meant pretending the abuse never happened.
You thought forgiveness meant giving someone access to your life simply because they knew how to say, “God wants you to forgive me.”
But forgiveness is not the same as reconciliation.
And reconciliation is not the same as trust.
You can refuse to hate someone without trusting them.
You can pray for someone's repentance without inviting them back into your home.
You can surrender your desire for personal revenge while still telling the truth about what happened.
You can desire their salvation and still recognize that their behavior makes close relationship unsafe.
That is not necessarily unforgiveness.
Sometimes it is wisdom.
Proverbs 22:3 says:
“A prudent man foreseeth the evil, and hideth himself: but the simple pass on, and are punished.” (KJV)
Wisdom does not become sin simply because someone is offended by your boundaries.
And Christian love does not require you to become a willing participant in your own repeated mistreatment.

If someone has abused you, threatened you, exploited you, or placed you in danger, seeking protection, involving appropriate authorities, and establishing firm boundaries are not betrayals of the Gospel.
Forgiveness does not erase accountability.
Grace does not eliminate consequences.
And the church must never use biblical language to pressure victims into silence.
But there is another side to this truth.
A side we cannot ignore merely because it is painful.
You may have every reason to keep someone at a distance.
But do you have biblical permission to feed hatred in your heart?
That is a different question.
Romans 12:19 says:
“Dearly beloved, avenge not yourselves, but rather give place unto wrath: for it is written, Vengeance is mine; I will repay, saith the Lord.” (KJV)
The Greek expression behind “avenge not yourselves” includes:
μὴ ἑαυτοὺς ἐκδικοῦντες — mē heautous ekdikountes
It is a prohibition against taking vengeance for ourselves.
Paul is not saying injustice is imaginary.
He is saying that final judgment does not belong to our wounded hands.
And that distinction can be agonizing.
Because sometimes what we call justice is really a desperate desire to make another person feel the pain they caused us.
We imagine the moment they finally understand.
The moment they finally cry.
The moment they finally lose what they took for granted.
The moment they experience the loneliness they left behind.
And beneath those thoughts is often a wounded heart crying out:
“Does anybody see what happened to me?”
God does.
That is one of the most important truths in this entire conversation.
God does not need your bitterness to remember your suffering.
He does not need your revenge to establish His justice.
He does not need you to pretend the wound never happened.
He already knows.
Every lie.
Every betrayal.
Every hidden conversation.
Every tear nobody witnessed.
Every night you asked Him why someone you loved could treat you so cruelly.
Nothing escapes His sight.
But neither does the condition of your own heart.
And sometimes, while we are waiting for another person to repent, resentment begins quietly reshaping us.
We become suspicious of everyone.
We punish people who never harmed us.
We rehearse old conversations until yesterday's pain becomes today's identity.
We tell ourselves we are protecting our hearts, but slowly discover that the person who hurt us still occupies enormous space in our thoughts.
They may no longer be in the room.
Yet their offense still seems to control the atmosphere.
This is why Jesus' teaching on forgiveness is not an invitation to deny reality.
It is a summons to freedom from the tyranny of vengeance.
But freedom is not always instantaneous.
Sometimes surrender begins with a prayer so small it barely sounds spiritual.
“Lord, I do not want to forgive them.”
Not impressive.
Not polished.
Not something you would proudly post online.
Just the truth.
“Lord, I am angry.”
“Lord, I still want them to suffer.”
“Lord, I know what Your Word says, but I do not know how to obey it without feeling like I am betraying myself.”
And perhaps the most honest prayer of all:
“Jesus, I am willing for You to make me willing.”
That is not a magic formula.
It is a beginning.
Because genuine Christian transformation is not manufactured by pretending to possess emotions we do not have.
It grows as the Holy Spirit brings our hearts under the truth and grace of Christ.
Now consider something extraordinary.
When Jesus was being crucified, Luke records Him saying:
“Father, forgive them; for they know not what they do.” (Luke 23:34, KJV)
The Greek wording is:
Πάτερ, ἄφες αὐτοῖς — Pater, aphes autois
“Father, forgive them.”

There is an important textual detail here. Some early Greek manuscripts omit this sentence, while many others include it. Most Christian Bibles retain it, sometimes with a textual note. Its presence is therefore discussed in New Testament textual criticism.
Even with that qualification, the prayer reflects a mercy consistent with Jesus' teaching to love enemies.
Consider the scene.
Jesus is not surrounded by people offering apologies.
He is being mocked.
Rejected.
Humiliated.
Crucified.
Yet He prays for mercy.
Notice, however, that His prayer does not mean every person involved in the crucifixion was automatically reconciled to God regardless of repentance or faith.
In Acts 2, Peter confronts his hearers with their responsibility concerning Jesus' death and calls them to repent.
The mercy of Christ is not opposed to repentance.
His mercy opens the way for sinners to turn to God.
And this brings us to the center of the Gospel.
We cannot understand Christian forgiveness by looking only at the person who hurt us.
We must look at the Savior who died for sinners.
Romans 5:8 declares:
“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.” (KJV)
While we were yet sinners.
Not after we had cleaned up our lives.
Not after we had become worthy.
Not after we had accumulated enough religious achievements to impress heaven.
Christ died for sinners.
But Scripture also calls people to repent and believe the Gospel.
Mark 1:15 records Jesus saying:
“The time is fulfilled, and the kingdom of God is at hand: repent ye, and believe the gospel.” (KJV)
God's love in sending Christ precedes our repentance.
Yet receiving the saving benefits of Christ is not presented as a license to remain defiantly opposed to Him.
Grace is free to the undeserving.
It is not permission to cherish sin.
And here is the breathtaking truth.
Jesus does not ask you to extend mercy because evil does not matter.
He calls you to mercy because you yourself live by mercy.
Ephesians 4:32 says:
“And be ye kind one to another, tenderhearted, forgiving one another, even as God for Christ's sake hath forgiven you.” (KJV)
The Greek includes the expression:
χαριζόμενοι ἑαυτοῖς — charizomenoi heautois
The verb charizomai carries the sense of graciously giving or forgiving.
It is related to charis, the Greek word commonly translated “grace.”
That connection is beautiful.
Christian forgiveness is meant to reflect grace.
Not moral indifference.
Not the destruction of boundaries.
Not the denial of justice.
Grace.
The kind of grace that looks at a guilty sinner and recognizes that salvation is not something any of us can purchase.
The kind of grace that refuses to let another person's sin become an excuse for our own.
The kind of grace that teaches us to release revenge even when repentance has not yet appeared.
And still, there is a warning here.
Because the Bible does not allow us to turn forgiveness into a convenient religious performance.
Jesus told a disturbing parable in Matthew 18 about a servant who received extraordinary mercy from his master but then treated a fellow servant mercilessly over a much smaller debt.
The point was not that human offenses are trivial.
The point was that people who have received immeasurable mercy from God must not cultivate a merciless spirit toward others.
Jesus concluded with a serious warning about refusing to forgive from the heart.
That should humble every one of us.
But we must also read the passage in context.
Earlier in Matthew 18, Jesus taught His disciples to confront a sinning brother, involve witnesses when necessary, and take persistent unrepentance seriously.
In the very chapter that calls us to forgive repeatedly, Jesus also teaches accountability.
He does not present forgiveness as a substitute for truth.
And He does not present accountability as permission for hatred.
Both belong within the life of His people.
This is why the question, “Must I forgive someone who has never repented?” deserves a careful answer.
Yes, Christians are commanded to cultivate a forgiving, merciful heart, relinquish personal vengeance, love their enemies, and remain willing to extend forgiveness.
But Scripture does not require us to declare an unrepentant person reconciled, restore broken trust without evidence of change, or continue exposing ourselves to harm.
Whether one describes the inward release of resentment as forgiveness itself or as the disposition of forgiveness, the practical biblical obligations remain serious.
Love must not disappear.
Truth must not disappear.
Wisdom must not disappear.
And repentance must not be treated as meaningless.
That is not a compromise between holiness and compassion.
It is an attempt to honor everything Scripture teaches.
Now let me ask you something personal.
What if the person who hurt you never apologizes?
Not next month.
Not next year.
Not even on their deathbed.
What if they spend the rest of their life convinced they were right?
What if they tell everyone a version of the story in which you are the villain?
What if the confession you have waited years to hear never comes?
Will your peace remain permanently chained to a sentence they may never speak?
That question is painful because it exposes something many of us secretly believe.
“If they would just admit what they did, I could finally heal.”
And an honest apology can indeed be deeply meaningful.
Confession matters.
Repentance matters.
Restitution, where possible, matters.
Justice matters.
But your spiritual life cannot depend entirely upon another person's willingness to tell the truth.
Because then the person who wounded you would hold a kind of authority over your future that belongs to God alone.
There is a difference between waiting for reconciliation and waiting for permission to live again.
You may never receive the apology.
You may never see the repentance.
You may never recover everything you lost.
But by God's grace, your story does not have to end at the place where somebody betrayed you.
The cross means evil does not get the final word.
The resurrection means death does not get the final word.
And Jesus Christ is able to bring redemption into a life that still carries scars.
Not by pretending the scars were never there.
But by proving that scars do not have to define the whole person.
After His resurrection, Jesus showed His disciples His wounded hands and side.
The risen Savior was not presented as someone whose suffering had been meaningless.
His wounds testified to the price of redemption.
That does not mean every human wound will produce an easily explained purpose.
Some suffering remains profoundly mysterious.
But it does mean that the God who saves us is not unfamiliar with betrayal, injustice, abandonment, or pain.
He knows what it means to be rejected.
He knows what it means to be falsely accused.
He knows what it means to suffer at the hands of sinners.
And He is not indifferent to your tears.
So perhaps today, your next step is not to call the person who hurt you.
Perhaps it is not to send a message.
Perhaps it is not to reopen a relationship that has repeatedly proven destructive.
Perhaps your next step is simply to kneel before Jesus and say:
“Lord, I surrender my right to personal revenge.”
“I ask You to judge rightly.”
“I ask You to deal with the person who hurt me.”
“If they need repentance, bring them to repentance.”
“If I need correction, correct me.”
“If I need protection, give me wisdom.”
“If there is a righteous path toward reconciliation, guide us into truth.”
“And if reconciliation never happens, do not let hatred become the master of my heart.”
That prayer does not erase consequences.
It does not guarantee an immediate feeling of relief.
It does not mean that trauma, grief, or broken trust will disappear overnight.
Some wounds require time, wise pastoral care, professional support, and patient healing.
But it places your suffering before the One who can be trusted with both mercy and justice.
And perhaps there is something else we need to confess.
Sometimes we are not only the wounded person in the story.
Sometimes we are the one who did the wounding.
We remember the conversation we twisted.
The promise we broke.
The apology we withheld because our pride would not allow us to admit the truth.
The person we blamed because accepting responsibility felt unbearable.
We know how to explain our behavior.
We know how to defend our intentions.
We know how to describe the circumstances that made our choices understandable.
But deep inside, we know we sinned.
And we have been hoping that enough time would make repentance unnecessary.
If that is you, hear this carefully.
Do not use an article about forgiveness to demand that someone overlook your unrepentance.
Do not weaponize the grace of God against someone you have harmed.
Do not say, “The Bible says you must forgive me,” while refusing to confess what you did.
Jesus did not die so that we could become more sophisticated at avoiding accountability.
He died to save sinners and transform them.
Repentance is not merely saying, “Sorry you were hurt.”
It is honestly acknowledging wrongdoing, turning away from it, and seeking to make things right where possible.
And even sincere repentance does not entitle you to immediate restoration of trust.
The person you hurt may need distance.
They may need evidence of lasting change.
Some consequences may remain.
You can be forgiven by God through Christ and still be responsible for repairing what you can.
That is not a failure of grace.
That is part of taking sin seriously.
And if you are the one who has been hurt, remember this too.
Your offender's repentance is not something you can manufacture.
You cannot argue someone into genuine sorrow.
You cannot control the Holy Spirit's work in another person's heart.
You cannot make a person love truth by sacrificing your own well-being.
You can speak truth.
You can establish boundaries.
You can pray.
You can seek appropriate help.
You can entrust justice to God.
And you can continue following Jesus.
Even before they change.
Especially if they never do.
This is where the Gospel becomes more than a comforting religious phrase.
It becomes the foundation beneath your feet when the apology never arrives.
It becomes the light that helps you recognize the difference between mercy and enabling.
It becomes the courage to confess your own sin without excusing someone else's.
It becomes the strength to pursue peace without surrendering truth.
It becomes the reminder that your identity is not “the person who was betrayed.”
Your deepest identity, if you belong to Christ, is someone redeemed by His blood, adopted by His grace, and called to walk in newness of life.
The scandal of sin is real.
The devastation of betrayal is real.
The seriousness of repentance is real.
But so is the grace of Jesus Christ.
And grace is not weak.
Grace is what brings proud sinners to their knees.
Grace is what teaches wounded hearts to stop worshiping revenge.
Grace is what makes confession possible.
Grace is what gives forgiveness its meaning.
Grace is what reminds us that the final chapter belongs to Jesus, not to the person who hurt us.
This is why Gospel Warrior exists.
Not to entertain people with religious words for a few passing moments.
Not to turn suffering into engagement statistics.
Not to make Christianity sound easier than Jesus said it would be.
But to keep bringing people back to Scripture, to repentance, to the cross, and to the hope of genuine transformation through Christ.
Because somewhere, someone is reading this while fighting a battle nobody sees.
A husband who still cannot understand his wife's betrayal.
A wife who has been told to forgive while her safety and dignity are repeatedly violated.
A son who grew up waiting for a father to admit what he did.
A daughter who has spent years believing that honoring her parents means denying her own pain.
A friend who was discarded.
A believer who feels ashamed because the wound still hurts.
And perhaps someone who has committed a terrible wrong and is finally beginning to understand the need for repentance.
These are not imaginary struggles.
They are real lives.
Real tears.
Real souls in need of biblical truth.
If this message has helped you see the difference between forgiveness, repentance, reconciliation, and trust, please do not let it end with you.
There is a world of difference between a social media page that merely collects attention and a community that continually directs people toward Jesus Christ.
We want to keep building the latter.
Those resources are part of our desire to make biblical encouragement and discipleship accessible, including to people who may not have the means to pay.
Not because God measures your faithfulness by whether you support this particular ministry.
And certainly not because salvation, forgiveness, or God's favor can be purchased.
They cannot.
Salvation is by grace through faith in Jesus Christ, not by financial contribution.
But Scripture does teach that believers may voluntarily support those who faithfully serve through the ministry of the Word.
Galatians 6:6 says:
“Let him that is taught in the word communicate unto him that teacheth in all good things.” (KJV)
And 2 Corinthians 9:7 reminds us:
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.” (KJV)
That is the spirit in which we invite support.
Not pressure.
Not guilt.
Not a promise of financial miracles in exchange for money.
But a willing partnership in making Christ-centered teaching available to more people.
It is not a biblically required tithe, nor a replacement for responsibilities to your local church, your family, or those in need.
It is an additional opportunity to give toward a ministry you believe is serving others faithfully.
Those items are simply a token of appreciation.
You are no less welcome.
You can still read, pray, learn, share, and grow with us.
Your worth before God is not measured by your ability to give.
Not because reading it once will automatically heal years of pain.
But because there may come another night when the memories return, the anger rises, and you need to remember what Scripture actually says.
And before you leave, I want to ask you something.
Not a question for the sake of collecting comments.
A question worth bringing honestly before God.
Are you struggling to forgive someone who has never apologized, or are you realizing that you owe someone a sincere repentance of your own?
You can simply write, “Jesus, help me surrender what I cannot change.”
Or write, “I'm still healing.”
And if you have a testimony of how Christ helped you release bitterness without abandoning truth, consider sharing it. Your experience may encourage someone who feels completely alone.
There is no need to pretend you have reached a place of peace you have not yet reached.
Bring the truth of your heart to Jesus.
Because He is not merely interested in changing your public appearance.
He came to redeem your life.
He came to forgive sinners.
He came to call the unrepentant to repentance.
He came to reconcile people to God.
He came to make all things new.
And one day, the justice of God will be revealed without error, without corruption, and without a single overlooked wrong.
Until then, we walk by faith.
We speak truth.
We pursue peace where possible.
We establish wise boundaries where necessary.
We refuse personal vengeance.
We extend mercy.
We repent when we sin.
We forgive as people who have been forgiven.
And we keep our eyes fixed on Jesus Christ.
So, does the Bible require you to forgive someone who has never repented?
It requires more than pretending everything is fine.
It calls you to a heart that refuses to be ruled by revenge, a love that can pray even for enemies, and a willingness to extend mercy without compromising truth.
It does not require you to manufacture reconciliation where repentance is absent.
It does not require you to rebuild trust where trustworthiness has not been demonstrated.
And it never requires you to call darkness light.
Your calling is not to become the judge of another person's soul.
Your calling is to remain faithful to the Savior who knows both the wound you suffered and the mercy you yourself need.
And perhaps that is where healing begins.
Not when they finally say they are sorry.
Not when the past suddenly makes sense.
Not when every consequence disappears.
But when you discover that your future is no longer waiting for your offender to give you permission to live.
The apology may never come—but the risen Christ is still able to lead you out of the place where their sin left you.
